title: The Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:1–13)
hook: the youngest son, out with the sheep, is chosen and anointed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mizpeh, where Saul hid among the baggage. Your line was come out from the baggage.

An old prophet is grieving, and God tells him to stop: "How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? fill thine horn with oil, and go." The tall king from yesterday has gone wrong, and Samuel can't let go of him. He's sent to Bethlehem, to Jesse, grandson of Ruth and Boaz. Samuel is afraid: "How can I go? if Saul hear it, he will kill me." So he goes quietly, with a heifer for a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and his sons. One of them is about to be anointed king. Samuel doesn't know which.
screen: `HOW LONG WILT THOU MOURN FOR SAUL?`

segments.voice: Jesse's son Eliab walks in first, and Samuel thinks he's found him: "Surely the LORD'S anointed is before him." God answers with the line that names today: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Yesterday the crowd cheered a king taller than everyone from the shoulders up. Samuel is about to be drawn by height again, and God stops him. The sons pass by: "Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. And Samuel said unto Jesse, The LORD hath not chosen these." Then: "Are here all thy children?" Jesse admits, "There remaineth yet the youngest, and, behold, he keepeth the sheep." Nobody thought to call him in. Samuel says, we will not sit down till he comes. Until now, the story hasn't said his name. He arrives, and the text, with a little smile, describes him anyway: "ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to." The point was never that looks are bad. It's that they aren't what God goes by. "Arise, anoint him: for this is he." Samuel pours the oil in front of his brothers, and only then does the name appear: "the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward." Samuel goes home to Ramah. Nothing in these verses makes the boy king yet.
screen: `SURELY THE LORD'S ANOINTED IS BEFORE HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you've sized up by the outside, their clothes, age, accent, job, the way they talk: someone you'd have left out with the sheep. Hold their face for a moment and try to look past it: what do you actually know of their heart? If you pray, ask to see them the way the text says God sees.
Eliab. Jesse's eldest son, whom Samuel almost anointed before God said, man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
Your line: god looks on the heart. The one left with the sheep was the one. That's day seven hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Christians read 1 Samuel 16:7 as a reminder that God does not judge by appearance, and read the anointing of the youngest son alongside other stories in scripture where God chooses the overlooked.

chat.says: Why didn't God choose the tall, impressive brother Samuel liked?
options: Because the LORD looks on the heart, not on the outward appearance.
Because Eliab had broken a law, and Samuel found out just in time.
Because Jesse wanted his youngest son to rule, and asked Samuel.

notes: 'Has gone wrong' summarizes 1 Samuel 13–15 (Saul's rejection in 15:23–26), skipped by the outline.

'Seven of his sons' is 16:10. Whether that seven includes Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah (16:6–9) is left unstated; 1 Chronicles 2:13–15 lists David as the seventh son, an apparent tension the script avoids.
'Until now the story hasn't said his name': David is unnamed in 16:1–12 and first named in 16:13; confirm.

Audit: "make the same choice twice" and the trapdoor's "the mistake of Saul's height" implied Samuel chose Saul for his height; the text has Saul chosen by the LORD (9:16–17) and by lot (10:20–24). Now "drawn by height again". "Nothing in the chapter" narrowed to "these verses" (16:14–23 continues the chapter).
Editor 2: removed 'the eldest' for Eliab in teach and myth (1 Samuel 16 does not say it; 17:13 and 17:28 do).
Editor: replaced 'and the boy goes back to the sheep', which 16:13 does not say, with Samuel's return to Ramah (16:13, paraphrased).
(Superseded) 'And the boy goes back to the sheep' anticipated 16:19 ('David thy son, which is with the sheep'); confirm it does not teach tomorrow's story too early.
